title: WSD learning-rate schedules
summary: Why warmup-stable-decay replaced cosine for many LLM runs: how a long constant LR phase plus a short cooldown matches cosine, why the loss plunges in the decay, and how it makes scaling studies cheap.
outcomes: Explain why cosine decay ties the learning-rate curve to a training length chosen in advance
Write down the WSD schedule and compute its LR at any step for linear and 1-sqrt cooldowns
Explain the sharp loss drop in the decay using the river valley picture
Choose cooldown length, shape and floor using published ablations
Plan a scaling study with one constant LR run per model size and branched cooldowns
Run a branched WSD experiment that restores weights, optimizer state, step and data order, and spot a weights-only resume
Compare cooldowns with checkpoint averaging and Schedule-Free AdamW, and pick a schedule for a known or unknown budget
Use the convex bound and the token-horizon law to adjust the peak LR when a run is extended

lessons.title: Why cosine forces you to fix the training length up front

blocks.md: In the prerequisite course you met warmup followed by **cosine decay**. For large language models (LLMs) it has been the default since GPT, OpenAI's 2018 model whose paper already lowered the learning rate along a cosine, and large models such as DeepMind's 280B-parameter Gopher and Meta's LLaMA used it too. After warmup, the learning rate (LR) typically decays to 10% of its peak. Hägele et al. (2024) call it the de-facto standard schedule. The decay phase is also called **annealing**, after the metalworking practice of cooling metal slowly: a run is fully annealed once its LR has come down to its small final value.

blocks.caption: Cosine decay to 10% of the peak eta max (warmup omitted); eta min is the floor. s is the current step and T the cycle length, the step where the LR reaches the floor. The cosine term falls from 1 at s = 0 to -1 at s = T, so the LR slides along half a cosine wave from peak to floor, then stays there.

blocks.md: At the halfway step $s = T/2$ the cosine is 0, so the LR is $0.1 + 0.45 = 0.55$ of peak: the floor plus half the gap. The catch is the single parameter $T$. The Chinchilla paper (Hoffmann et al., 2022), the DeepMind study that trained over 400 language models to work out how to split a compute budget between model size and training data, found that the best loss for a given number of training steps $S$ is reached only when $T$ matches $S$, and that overshooting $S$ by more than 25% clearly hurts. MiniCPM (Hu et al., 2024), a family of small language models whose paper introduced the schedule this course is about, reproduced this on a 0.036B-parameter model: for runs of 20 to 80 tokens per parameter (20N to 80N tokens for N parameters), the lowest loss always came from $T = S$; both $T < S$ and $T > S$ were worse.

blocks.title: Cosine to 10% with cycle length T, run stops at step S

scenes.caption: T = S: the LR reaches its 10% floor exactly when training ends. At the halfway point it is still 0.55 of peak, at 0.9 S it is 0.122.
T = 0.6 S: the LR hits the floor at 0.6 S and then crawls at 10% for the last 40% of training. Too little time at high LR.
T = 1.4 S: when training stops the LR is still well above the floor, so the run never fully anneals. Chinchilla saw clear damage beyond 25% overshoot.

blocks.title: Toy model: final loss above the floor of 2.0, by cycle length

scenes.caption: Computed with the simplified toy model from lesson 3, not a real LLM, 10,000 steps. T = S wins (0.554). Ending too early costs 0.020, overshooting by 40% costs 0.032, and never decaying (constant LR) costs 0.197.

blocks.md:
This coupling causes three practical problems:

1. **Mid-run checkpoints are underestimates.** A checkpoint is a saved copy of the weights, plus the optimizer's running averages (for Adam, the moving averages of each weight's gradient and squared gradient, which set the size of its next step), taken partway through training. Halfway through a cosine run the LR is still 55% of peak, so the checkpoint is worse than a model that was trained, and annealed, for that many tokens.
2. **Extending a run is awkward.** If more compute arrives after $T$, the LR is already at the floor, where progress is slow. Rewarming it, raising the LR back toward the peak, causes **loss spikes** (sudden jumps in the training loss) that recover slowly (Hägele et al.).
3. **Scaling studies get expensive.** A scaling study trains many models of different sizes on different amounts of data and fits a formula, a **scaling law**, that predicts loss from them. To learn how loss depends on data size, you need a separate run from scratch for every length.

blocks.prompt: Chinchilla's Approach 1, the first of its three ways to find the best model size, trained each model size (70M to 10B parameters) with four different cosine cycle lengths. If a study uses m model sizes and m data sizes, roughly how many training runs does it need with cosine?
blocks.reveal: About $m^2$: one run from scratch for every (model size, data size) pair, because each data size needs its own $T$. MiniCPM describes the cost as $O(m^2)C$ for an average per-run cost $C$. The rest of this course shows how a schedule that does not depend on $T$ brings this down to about $m$ long runs plus cheap short branches.

blocks.md: Cosine couples the **shape** of the LR curve to the **end date** of training. You must choose the training length before you start, and every checkpoint before the end is half-annealed.

blocks.question: A teammate evaluates the 50% checkpoint of a cosine run (T = S) and concludes that 'training on half the data gives loss X'. Why is X misleading?
options: The checkpoint has seen only half the data, so X is accurate by definition
The LR at that point is still about 0.55 of peak, so the model has not been annealed; a run with T equal to half the length would reach a lower loss
Cosine checkpoints are always better than fully trained models of the same length, so X is too optimistic
Weight decay has not taken effect yet at 50% of training
blocks.explain: Mid-run cosine checkpoints are underestimates. Most of the loss drop from annealing happens when the LR gets small, which for this run only happens near S. A cosine run with T set to the shorter length would anneal earlier and end lower.

blocks.question: You planned 100k steps with cosine (T = 100k), but the cluster time is cut and you must stop at 70k. Which outcome is most likely, compared with a run planned for 70k from the start?
options: Identical loss: the schedule only matters at the end
Lower loss, because the LR stayed high for longer
Higher loss, because at 70k the LR is still well above the floor and the run never annealed
blocks.explain: Stopping at 0.7 T is equivalent to a cycle that overshoots the stop by about 43%, the regime where Chinchilla reports clear degradation. The model has not had its low LR phase.

lessons.title: Warmup, stable, decay: the schedule and its loss curve

blocks.md: MiniCPM (Hu et al., 2024) split training explicitly into a high LR part and a decay part and named the result the **Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD)** schedule. Warmup ramps the LR up to the peak $\eta$ over $W$ steps. The **stable** stage holds the LR constant at $\eta$ until step $T$. The **decay** stage (also called the **cooldown** or annealing phase) lowers it with a decreasing function $f$ until the final step $S$.

blocks.tex: \mathrm{WSD}(s)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{s}{W}\,\eta & s<W\\[4pt] \eta & W\le s<T\\[4pt] f(s-T)\,\eta & T\le s\le S\end{cases}\qquad 0<f\le 1\ \text{decreasing}
blocks.caption: The WSD schedule as defined by MiniCPM. During warmup the LR is s over W times the peak, a straight ramp; from W to T it is the peak; after T it is the peak times f of the steps since T, where f starts at 1 and falls. T now marks the end of the stable stage, not a cosine cycle length.

blocks.md:
Hägele et al. (2024) studied the same shape under the name **constant LR + cooldown**, noting it had earlier been called a trapezoidal schedule (Zhai et al., 2022), since a ramp up, a flat top and a ramp down draw a trapezoid. The cooldown usually takes the LR to zero, mirroring the warmup. The key property: until the decay starts, the schedule does not depend on when training will end.

To compare schedules, this course uses the **area** under the LR curve: the sum of LR divided by the peak over all steps. Treat it as a modeling assumption, not a general fact: the toy model in lesson 3 and the Tissue et al. loss law there both assume that progress depends on the summed LR, and lesson 3 explains why. Ignoring warmup, holding the peak for 90% of training and ramping linearly to zero over the last 10% gives an area of $0.9 + 0.1/2 = 0.95$ times $S$; cosine to 10% gives $0.55$ times $S$, because its cosine term averages to zero over the cycle. Hägele et al. also use a **1-sqrt** cooldown, whose multiplier is 1 minus the square root of the fraction of the cooldown completed.

blocks.title: WSD with a cooldown of fraction F of training

scenes.caption: Cosine (grey) starts decaying right after warmup. WSD with linear cooldown over the last 20% holds the peak until 0.8 S, then falls straight to 0.
F = 0.1, the MiniCPM default: the LR stays at peak for 90% of training. Its area under the curve is 0.95 of the peak times S, versus 0.55 for cosine to 10%.
The 1-sqrt cooldown of Hägele et al. drops faster at first and lingers near zero longer. Halfway through the cooldown it is at 0.29 of peak, versus 0.5 for linear.

blocks.prompt: Two runs share the same peak LR and length. Run A uses cosine (T = S); run B uses WSD with a 10% cooldown. At 80% of training, run B has clearly higher loss than run A. Which run do you expect to end lower?
blocks.reveal: Neither wins by much, and B often edges ahead. MiniCPM reports that once the decay starts the loss drops sharply and quickly reaches a level equal to or lower than cosine at $T = S$. Hägele et al. found an almost perfect match between the best cosine and the best cooldown runs across lengths. The high loss during the stable stage hides progress that only the decay reveals.

blocks.title: Toy model: loss above 2.0 during training (10,000 steps)

scenes.caption: Step 2,000. Cosine has already started to lower its LR and is slightly ahead (0.822 vs 0.839). The three high LR runs are identical so far.
Step 5,000: cosine is at half its peak LR and leads by 0.100. A plot of these curves would make WSD look like the worse schedule.
Step 9,000: WSD with a 20% decay has been decaying for 1,000 steps and already dropped from 0.756 to 0.636. Cosine, at 0.562, is still ahead.
Step 9,500: WSD with a 10% decay starts its decay at 9,000 and falls from 0.756 to 0.638 in 500 steps.
Step 10,000: the 20% decay ends at 0.538 and the 10% decay at 0.550, both below cosine (0.554). Constant LR never anneals (0.750). Simplified: the toy exaggerates sharpness; real gaps are small.

blocks.md: Because the stable stage is independent of the end date, you can **branch**. Save checkpoints (weights plus optimizer state) along the stable stage. To get a finished model at any length, start a short cooldown from the nearest checkpoint. To train longer, resume the stable stage from the latest pre-decay checkpoint at the same peak LR. MiniCPM verified that continuing the stable stage and then decaying again reaches the same loss as a cosine run planned for the longer length.

blocks.title: One stable run, many finished models

scenes.caption: Warmup, then a single stable run at constant LR. Checkpoints are saved along the way; nothing about the run depends on a planned end.
A cooldown of about 10% of each model's total length is branched from each checkpoint. Each branch is a short side run; the main run keeps going at the peak LR.
Need a longer model later? Resume from the last stable checkpoint, not from a decayed model, so the LR never has to be rewarmed.

blocks.md: Hugging Face Transformers, the widely used open-source model library, ships this schedule as `get_wsd_schedule`. It takes the warmup, decay and either the stable or total step counts, a `decay_type` of `"linear"`, `"cosine"` (the default) or `"1-sqrt"`, and a `min_lr_ratio` floor that defaults to 0.

blocks.title: The WSD multiplier from Transformers, simplified to linear warmup

scenes.caption: Step 50 is in warmup: the factor is 50 / 100 = 0.5. With a peak LR of 3e-4 the optimizer uses 1.5e-4.
Step 400 is in the stable stage (100 to 799): factor 1.0, LR 3e-4. This branch does not depend on the total length at all.
Step 850: decay progress p = 50 / 200 = 0.25. The 1-sqrt shape gives 1 - 0.5 = 0.5, so the LR is already halved a quarter of the way into the cooldown.
Step 950: p = 0.75, f = 1 - sqrt(0.75) = 0.134, LR 4.02e-5. Linear would still be at 0.25.
Step 1000 and beyond: the function returns the floor, min_lr_ratio = 0.

blocks.question: You run WSD and save a checkpoint every 5k steps. At 60k steps you decide to train to 100k. Which checkpoint should you continue from?
options: The latest stable-stage checkpoint (60k), continuing at the same constant peak LR
The end of the 6k-step cooldown branch, rewarming the LR to peak
A fresh run from scratch with cosine and T = 100k
blocks.explain: The stable stage is the reusable trunk. Continuing it at the same LR needs no rewarm and later gets its own cooldown. (A variant that resumes from the decayed model, WSD-S, where the final S stands for simplified, appears in lesson 6, but plain WSD rolls back to the pre-decay checkpoint.)

lessons.title: Why the loss plunges during the decay: the river valley picture

blocks.md: Why would a run that looks worse for 90% of training catch up in the last 10%? Wen et al. (2024) propose that the pretraining loss looks like a **river valley**: a deep gorge with steep hillsides and a river winding along the bottom. Any loss value splits into a **river** component (how far along the valley you are) and a **hill** component (how high up the walls you are).

Stochastic gradients make the parameters bounce between the steep walls. With a high LR, the bouncing is large, so the hill component is high, but each step also moves further along the river. With a low LR, the iterate (the current parameter vector) sits near the bottom but crawls along it. Their conclusion: keep the LR high as long as possible to make river progress, then decay quickly to stop the bouncing and reveal that progress. Why measure river progress by the summed LR rather than by the step count? Along the river floor the gradient is small and points the same way step after step, so each step moves about $\eta$ times that gradient, and the distance travelled grows with $\sum \eta$. That is the assumption built into the toy below.

blocks.caption: Our own toy, constants picked by hand. u is LR / peak. Loss is a floor of 2, plus a river term, 1.25 times (S sub t plus 50) to the minus 0.1, that shrinks as S sub t, the area under the LR curve so far (not the run length S), grows. Then the hill H: excess loss from bouncing on one steep wall.

blocks.md: Where does the $H$ update come from? Look at one steep direction and let $y$ be the distance from the valley floor along it. The loss there is the quadratic $\frac{h}{2}y^2$, where the **curvature** $h$ (the second derivative) says how steep the wall is. Here $\eta$ is the learning rate at the current step; lesson 2 used $\eta$ for the peak, which from now on gets its own name, $\eta_{peak}$. A gradient step with noise is $y \leftarrow (1-\eta h)\,y + \eta\,\xi$: the true gradient $hy$ pulls $y$ toward 0, and the gradient noise $\xi$, with mean zero and variance $\sigma^2$, kicks it randomly.

blocks.caption: Square the step and average: the cross term averages to zero because the noise has mean zero and does not depend on y. Multiplying by h/2 turns the average squared distance into the expected excess loss H.

blocks.md: So each step the new hill is the old hill times the square of $1-\eta h$, plus fresh noise worth $h/2$ times $\eta^2\sigma^2$. Write $\eta = u\,\eta_{peak}$ and pick toy values $\eta_{peak} h = 0.02$ and $\frac{h}{2}\eta_{peak}^2\sigma^2 = 0.01$. That turns the update into the toy rule: each step multiplies the old hill by the square of $1 - 0.02u$ and adds new noise $0.01u^2$. The **steady state** $H^*$ is where the two balance and $H$ stops changing. The shrink removes a fraction $0.04u - 0.0004u^2$ of $H^*$ (one minus the square of $1 - 0.02u$, multiplied out), and that loss must equal the noise added, $0.01u^2$. Dividing by $0.04u - 0.0004u^2$ gives $H^* = 0.01u/(0.04 - 0.0004u)$: 0.2525 at the peak, 0.1256 at half the peak, 0.0250 at a tenth. The denominator stays close to 0.04, so $H^* \approx u/4$: **the hill height is roughly proportional to the LR.**

blocks.title: Watching the hill component settle as the LR drops
blocks.code:
H = 0.2525    # hill loss at peak LR (u = 1), steady state

def run(u, steps):
    global H
    for _ in range(steps):
        H = (1 - 0.02 * u) ** 2 * H + 0.01 * u * u

run(0.5, 25)   # halve the LR
run(0.5, 75)
run(0.1, 500)  # drop to 10% of peak
run(0.0, 100)  # LR = 0

scenes.caption: At constant peak LR the bouncing is in steady state: H = 0.2525. The stable stage never gets below this, which is why its loss curve looks flat.
Halve the LR. After 25 steps H has fallen to 0.2024: each step shrinks H by the factor 0.99^2 and adds less new noise.
After 100 steps at half LR, H = 0.1426, approaching the new steady state 0.1256. The drop is fast because the walls are steep.
At 10% of peak the shrink factor per step is only 0.998^2, so settling is slow: 500 steps bring H to 0.0409, still above its steady state 0.0250.
At LR 0 nothing moves: H stays 0.0409. A decay that is too abrupt freezes whatever bouncing is left.

blocks.md: A lower LR does not remove the hill instantly: the walls only pull the iterate down while it still takes steps of reasonable size. That is why the cooldown needs a minimum length. MiniCPM found a 2.5% decay falls short where 10% suffices.

blocks.title: Toy model at step 10,000: where the loss comes from

scenes.caption: Constant LR: the most river progress (0.498, area 1.0 x S) but the full hill (0.253).
Cosine (T = S): the hill is almost gone (0.026), but its area is only about 0.55 x S, so the river part is the worst, 0.528.
WSD, 10% decay: river 0.501 (area about 0.95 x S) and hill 0.050. Total 0.550, slightly below cosine's 0.554.
WSD, 20% decay: a little river progress traded for a lower hill (0.035). Total 0.538, the best of the four.

blocks.md: Real runs show the same signatures. MiniCPM tracked gradients in the decay of a 0.2B model: the gradient norm shrinks, successive gradients mostly point the same way (the cosine of the angle between them, a similarity score unrelated to the cosine schedule, is positive), and the estimated curvature along the path grows by an order of magnitude, consistent with settling into a minimum. Hägele et al. linearly interpolated the weights between a checkpoint before and after cooldown and found the loss falls smoothly along that line, as if the model slides into one connected basin.

Tissue et al. (2024) fit full loss curves with an empirical law in the same spirit. $S_1$ is the area under the LR curve (river progress) and $S_2$ is an **annealing area**: every drop in LR feeds a running momentum term that fades by a factor $\lambda$ (0.99 to 0.999) per step, so a drop keeps paying off for roughly $1/(1-\lambda)$, that is 100 to 1000, steps; $S_2$ sums that momentum over all steps. Fit on a constant and a cosine run, it predicted loss curves of unseen schedules, and it explains why cosine works best with $T = S$: shorter $T$ loses area, longer $T$ loses annealing.

blocks.caption: Scaling law with LR annealing (Tissue et al.). Loss is an irreducible floor L0, plus a power law A times S1 to the minus alpha that falls as the area grows, minus C times the annealing area S2. L0, A, C and alpha are fitted per setup.

blocks.title: S1 and S2 on a 10-step toy schedule, lambda = 0.9
blocks.code:
import math
lam = 0.9

def areas(eta):           # eta[0] = LR before step 1 (the peak)
    m = S1 = S2 = 0.0
    for i in range(1, len(eta)):
        m = lam * m + (eta[i-1] - eta[i])  # annealing momentum
        S1 += eta[i]                        # forward area
        S2 += m                             # annealing area
    return S1, S2

wsd = [1.0] * 9 + [0.5, 0.0]      # 8 steps at peak, 2-step cooldown
cos = [1.0] + [0.1 + 0.45 * (1 + math.cos(math.pi * i / 10))
               for i in range(1, 11)]   # cosine to 10%
print(areas(wsd), areas(cos))

scenes.caption: WSD, steps 1 to 8: the LR never drops, so the momentum m stays 0 and S2 stays 0. S1 grows by 1 per step to 8.
Step 9 is the first cooldown step: the LR falls by 0.5, so m = 0.9 x 0 + 0.5 = 0.5 and S2 = 0.5. S1 only grows by 0.5.
Step 10: another drop of 0.5 on top of the decayed old momentum, m = 0.9 x 0.5 + 0.5 = 0.95, so S2 = 1.45. All of WSD's S2 is earned in the cooldown.
Cosine has been dropping since step 1, so its momentum has time to build: S2 = 3.82 against 1.45. But its S1 is only 5.05 against WSD's 8.5.

blocks.title: S1 and S2 at realistic scale (lambda = 0.999)

scenes.caption: A 100,000-step run, halfway. S1 is divided by the run length N and S2 by 1/(1 - lambda) = 1000. Cosine has already earned 0.44 of S2; WSD has earned none.
Step 90,000, where WSD's cooldown begins. WSD leads on S1 (0.90 vs 0.54), cosine on S2 (0.87 vs 0).
Step 95,000, halfway through the cooldown: WSD's S2 has jumped to 0.40 in 5,000 steps.
End of run: S2 is equal (0.90 each), while S1 is 0.95 for WSD vs 0.55 for cosine. The cooldown was 10 memory lengths long, enough to earn its S2 in full.
The same schedules on a 10,000-step run: the 1,000-step cooldown is only one memory length, so WSD ends with S2 = 0.37 vs 0.86 for cosine. A too-short cooldown leaves S2 unearned.

blocks.md: Read the law with these numbers. Constant LR maximizes $S_1$ but earns no $S_2$; cosine earns $S_2$ all along but gives up almost half of $S_1$; WSD keeps nearly all of $S_1$ and, if its cooldown is long compared with the $1/(1-\lambda)$ memory of the momentum, earns about as much $S_2$ as cosine. Tissue et al. reach the same conclusion: WSD and multi-step schedules give up a little $S_2$ for much more $S_1$, and during the cooldown the $S_2$ term causes most of the loss drop. Which schedule wins in the end depends on the fitted constants $A$, $\alpha$ and $C$.

blocks.question: In the river valley picture, why is the loss during the stable stage a bad indicator of how good the model will be after cooldown?
options: Because the validation set changes between stages
Because the high LR keeps the hill component elevated, hiding river progress that the decay will reveal
Because the stable stage only learns embeddings
Because the loss is computed with dropout on during the stable stage
blocks.explain: Loss = river + hill. A high LR inflates the hill part through bouncing between steep walls, so the plateau mostly reflects noise level, not lack of progress. The decay removes the hill part and the accumulated river progress shows up.

blocks.question: Using the toy numbers, a colleague proposes a 'cooldown' that drops the LR from peak straight to 0 in a single step at the end. What happens to the loss?
options: It falls to the river part, the best possible result
It explodes, because the LR changed too fast
It barely changes: with LR 0 no steps are taken, so the hill part stays where it was
blocks.explain: The hill only shrinks while the optimizer keeps taking steps at a moderate LR. With an instant drop to zero, H stays at its peak LR value of about 0.25. This is the extreme case of a too-short cooldown.

lessons.title: Tuning the cooldown: length, shape, floor and data

blocks.md: **Length.** MiniCPM decayed from stable checkpoints at 40, 60 and 80 tokens per parameter (40N, 60N, 80N) and found that a decay of 10% of total tokens gave the best results, while 2.5% fell short. Hägele et al. found the benefit of a longer cooldown plateaus at around 20% and that the cooldown beats cosine somewhere between 10% and 20%. Wen et al. saw final losses match tightly for decay fractions from 8% to 12%.

blocks.title: Toy model: final loss above 2.0 vs cooldown fraction

scenes.caption: Linear cooldown. 1% and 2.5% leave bouncing behind (0.649, 0.598). Cosine at T = S scores 0.554, matched at about 10% (0.550). Gains flatten from 20% to 50% (0.538 to 0.535).
1-sqrt cooldown, same budget. It is better at every fraction up to 30%, for example 0.539 vs 0.550 at 10%, because it gets the LR low early and spends longer letting the hill settle.

blocks.md: Hägele et al. add an important nuance: the fraction needed shrinks for long runs, as long as the cooldown is long enough in absolute steps. On a 200k-step run, a 10k-step (5%) 1-sqrt cooldown almost perfectly matched cosine.

**Shape.** Hägele et al. tested several decay functions and found that **1-sqrt** consistently beats linear, with the gap growing for longer runs. With $n$ the current step, $N$ the total steps (here $N$ counts steps, as in the $S_1/N$ bars of lesson 3, not parameters as in lesson 1) and $N_{decay}$ the cooldown length, the cooldown starts at step $N - N_{decay}$, so $p$ below is the fraction of the cooldown completed, from 0 to 1:

blocks.caption: At p = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 the 1-sqrt factor is 0.5, 0.293, 0.134; linear gives 0.75, 0.5, 0.25. The average LR over the cooldown is 1/3 for 1-sqrt (the average of the square root of p over 0 to 1 is 2/3, and 1 minus 2/3 is 1/3) and 1/2 for linear.

blocks.md: **Floor.** Hägele et al. kept the cosine baseline at the common 10% floor and found that decaying cosine lower improves loss to match the best 1-sqrt cooldown. They also saw that annealing all the way to zero can hurt some downstream benchmarks (tests of the finished model on tasks such as question answering, rather than its training loss), and recommend sweeping the peak and final LR independently. Chinchilla, by contrast, found 10x decay (down to a tenth of the peak) slightly better than decay to 0 in its setup. Treat the floor as a knob to tune, not a constant.

blocks.title: LR / peak in each tenth of training, three production-style schedules

scenes.caption: Cosine to 10%, sampled at the midpoint of each tenth: 0.951 already in the second tenth, 0.48 by the sixth, and under 0.25 for the last three tenths.

DeepSeek LLM (DeepSeek's 7B and 67B models, 2024) multi-step: peak until 80% of tokens, then 31.6% of peak, then 10% after 90%. Since 0.316 is 10 to the power -0.5, the two steps are equal on a log scale.
WSD with a 10% linear cooldown to 0 (MiniCPM-style length): peak for nine tenths, then a ramp whose midpoint is 0.5.

blocks.md: **Other decay forms in practice.** DeepSeek LLM used the multi-step schedule above (warmup of 2000 steps, then 80% / 10% / 10% stages) and reported final performance essentially matching cosine while letting the first stage be reused for continual training. MiniCPM-2.4B used exponential annealing, $f = 0.5^{(s-T)/T_h}$, where $s$ is the current step and $T$ the start of the decay, so the LR halves every $T_h$ steps. The half-life $T_h$ was 5000 steps (about 20B tokens at its 3.93M-token batch, since 5000 x 3.93M is about 19.7B), after about 1T tokens of stable training at a peak LR of 0.01.

**Data.** The cooldown is also a natural point to change the data mixture. MiniCPM mixed high-quality and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data, the prompt and answer pairs normally used after pretraining to teach a model to follow instructions, into the pretraining data only during the decay stage, and found this beat decaying on pretraining data alone. Hägele et al. note that Llama 3 (Meta, 2024) used annealing on specific data to assess data quality: run a short cooldown with a candidate dataset mixed in, and judge the data by how much the annealed model improves.

**Mid-training: OLMo 2 as a worked case.** OLMo 2 (2025) from Ai2, the Allen Institute for AI,, a family of fully open models, splits base training into two stages. Stage 1, pretraining, takes 90 to 95% of the training compute. Stage 2, which the authors call **mid-training** (5 to 10%), restarts from the stage 1 checkpoint and decays the LR linearly to zero on a different, smaller mix, **Dolmino Mix 1124**: up-sampled high-quality web pages, curated non-web sources and math data, including synthetic math built to patch weak math skills. The cooldown has become a stage of its own, with its own dataset. Stage 1 is not a pure constant LR. For the 7B and 32B models it runs a cosine schedule planned for a longer horizon (5T and 6.5T tokens) and cuts it off early (at 4T and 6T), so stage 2 starts above the 10% floor, at about 19% of peak for the 7B. The 13B ran its cosine to the end.

blocks.title: OLMo 2 7B: one pretrained trunk, three anneals, one soup

scenes.caption: Stage 1 trains on the large general mix. Its LR is still well above zero when it stops.
Stage 2 branches three anneals from the same checkpoint: same Dolmino mix, different data orders, each driving the LR linearly to zero over 50B tokens.
The three annealed models are averaged weight by weight (souped). In OLMo 2's comparisons the soup equaled or beat the best single anneal on almost every benchmark.

blocks.md: Two more tricks ride on the anneal. **Souping**: for the 7B model, OLMo 2 runs the 50B-token anneal three times with different random data orders and averages the three resulting weights; the 13B and 32B models average three 100B-token anneals and one 300B-token anneal. OLMo 2 reports that averaging runs on the same mix but with different data orders consistently equals or beats the best individual run (its own table shows one exception: on one trial mix the soup scored 17.5 points lower on a 200-problem subset of GSM8K, a benchmark of grade-school math word problems). **Microannealing**: to judge a candidate math source cheaply, they mix it 50/50 with general web data and run a short anneal; 19 such microanneals cost 130B tokens in total, less than the three 50B-token soup ingredients of the 7B model. Which mixture to anneal on is a data question of its own, beyond this course.

blocks.question: Your WSD run uses a 2% linear cooldown, and the final model is noticeably worse than a cosine baseline of the same length. What is the most likely fix?
options: Raise the peak LR so the stable stage makes more progress
Skip the cooldown and use the last stable checkpoint
Switch the cooldown to an LR increase
Lengthen the cooldown to roughly 10 to 20% of training, or at least enough absolute steps
blocks.explain: A very short cooldown leaves the hill component frozen in place (MiniCPM: 2.5% falls short, 10% enough; Hägele: gains plateau near 20%). A higher peak LR would only raise the hill further.

blocks.question: Why can 1-sqrt beat linear for the same cooldown length?
options: It reaches low LR earlier in the cooldown, giving more steps for the bouncing to settle, at the cost of a little river progress
It keeps the LR near peak for longer during the cooldown
It never reaches zero, so the model keeps learning
It is identical to cosine to 10%
blocks.explain: Halfway through the cooldown 1-sqrt is at 0.293 of peak versus 0.5 for linear. Its average LR over the cooldown is 1/3 versus 1/2, so it gives up some area (river progress) in exchange for more time at small LR to shrink the hill part.

blocks.question: OLMo 2 runs three 50B-token anneals of the same 7B checkpoint on the same mix and averages them. Why can averaging these work, when averaging two independently pretrained models usually would not?
options: Averaging always works for any two models of the same architecture
Each anneal uses a different LR, so averaging gives the best LR
The three anneals start from the same weights and stay close to each other, so their average lies in the same low-loss basin and cancels part of each run's data-order noise
The average is only used for evaluation; the released model is the first anneal
blocks.explain: The ingredients share a starting point and differ only by data order, so they stay near one another and averaging cancels part of each run's noise, the same idea as checkpoint averaging in lesson 7. Wortsman et al., whose model soups OLMo 2 cites, observed that models fine-tuned from the same pretrained weights often lie in a single low-error basin; nothing guarantees that for independently trained networks.

lessons.title: Run it yourself: one stable trunk, three cooldown branches

blocks.md:
Time to run the branching workflow yourself. The setup is small enough for a laptop: a character-level GPT, one whose tokens are single characters (4 transformer layers, width 128, 0.83M parameters) trained on Tiny Shakespeare, a 1.1M-character public text file, split 90/10 into training and validation text. Each step sees 32 sequences of 128 characters, and AdamW is the optimizer. On an Apple-silicon laptop GPU (PyTorch's MPS backend) every run in this lesson takes minutes; a CPU also works, only slower.

The plan: models finished at 2,000, 4,000 and 6,000 steps. WSD trains one stable trunk and branches a cooldown of 20% of each target length from it. The baseline trains three separate cosine runs, each with $T$ equal to its length.

blocks.caption: The LR multiplier is a plain function of the global step, the same idea as an lr_lambda for PyTorch's LambdaLR. decay_start is a parameter, so the trunk passes a start that never comes and each branch passes its own.

blocks.md:
A branch is only valid if it continues exactly where the trunk was. The prerequisite course showed that a resumable checkpoint holds the whole training state; for branching, four pieces matter:

1. **Weights.**
2. **Optimizer state**: AdamW's running averages $m$ and $v$ of each weight's gradient and squared gradient, plus its step count.
3. **The step counter** that drives the schedule, so the cooldown starts at the right LR and the right place.
4. **Data order**: here the state of the random generator that samples batches; with a file-based loader, its position. Without it a branch replays or skips data relative to the trunk.

blocks.code:
def save(m, opt, gen, step):          # everything a valid branch needs
    return {"step": step, "model": copy.deepcopy(m.state_dict()),
            "opt": copy.deepcopy(opt.state_dict()), "data_rng": gen.get_state()}

def branch(ckpt, total, shape="1-sqrt"):
    m, opt, gen = fresh()                # new model, AdamW and generator
    m.load_state_dict(ckpt["model"])
    opt.load_state_dict(ckpt["opt"])     # Adam's m, v and step count
    gen.set_state(ckpt["data_rng"])       # continue the same data stream
    s = ckpt["step"]                      # the schedule resumes at step s
    run(m, opt, gen, s, total, lambda t: wsd(t, s, total - s, shape))
    return evaluate(m)

m, opt, gen = fresh(); ckpts, step = {}, 0
for s in [1600, 3200, 4800]:             # one stable trunk
    run(m, opt, gen, step, s, lambda t: wsd(t, 10**9, 1)); step = s
    ckpts[s] = save(m, opt, gen, s)
for L, s in zip([2000, 4000, 6000], [1600, 3200, 4800]):
    print(L, branch(ckpts[s], L))        # three cooldown branches
blocks.caption: Checkpoints live in memory here; a real run saves them with torch.save. Not shown: the model (4 pre-norm nn.TransformerEncoderLayer blocks, causal mask, no dropout), batches at random offsets from a seeded torch.Generator, AdamW with betas (0.9, 0.95) and weight decay 0.1, and the cosine runs.

blocks.title: Training steps actually spent for the three models

scenes.caption: Cosine: three runs from scratch, 2,000 + 4,000 + 6,000 = 12,000 steps.
WSD: a 4,800-step trunk with checkpoints at 1,600, 3,200 and 4,800, then cooldowns of 400, 800 and 1,200 steps. Total 7,200 steps, 0.6x the cosine cost.

blocks.prompt: At step 4,800 the WSD trunk has validation loss 1.550 (nats per character). Its 1,200-step 1-sqrt cooldown ends at step 6,000, as does the 6,000-step cosine run. Which ends lower, and by roughly how much does the cooldown move the trunk?
blocks.reveal: The cooldown takes the trunk from 1.550 to 1.492, a drop of 0.058 in 1,200 steps, and ends below cosine's 1.513. The plateau of the trunk hid that progress, as in lesson 3's river valley.

blocks.title: Validation loss above 1.40 (nats per character), peak LR 2e-3

scenes.caption: The plunge, measured: each cooldown branch ends well below the trunk checkpoint it started from (1.660 to 1.575, 1.574 to 1.501, 1.550 to 1.492).

blocks.title: WSD branches vs separate cosine runs (val loss above 1.40)

scenes.caption: Seed 0, peak LR 2e-3 for both. WSD is lower at every length: by 0.050, 0.023 and 0.021, while costing 0.6x the steps.
A second seed (new initialization and data order): 1.624 vs 1.570, 1.536 vs 1.500, 1.513 vs 1.490. Same ordering.

blocks.md: How to read these numbers honestly. **LR sweep.** Both schedules were also run at peaks of 1e-3 and 4e-3. Taking each schedule's best LR at each length, cosine reaches 1.552, 1.500 and 1.513 and WSD 1.522, 1.478 and 1.489: WSD stays lower by 0.02 to 0.03. Cosine's best peak drops from 4e-3 to 2e-3 at 6,000 steps, a hint of lesson 7's horizon effect, but that gap (0.011) is at the noise level below. **Floor.** The cosine runs stop at 10% of peak and the cooldowns at zero; lesson 4 noted that a lower cosine floor closes much of such a gap. **Shape.** 1-sqrt and linear cooldowns ended within 0.002 of each other at peak 2e-3 (both seeds) and within 0.006 across the whole sweep. **Noise.** Repeating a run on the laptop GPU gives results that differ by about 0.01, because MPS kernels are not bit-for-bit deterministic, so treat smaller gaps as noise. **Scale.** 6,000 steps of 4,096 characters is about 24 passes over the training text, unlike LLM pretraining, which rarely repeats data. The lesson is the workflow, not the exact gap.

Now the classic branching bug, in a separate rerun of the same trunk (MPS noise puts its step-3,200 loss at 1.563 instead of 1.574, and its 800-step branch ends near 1.490 instead of 1.501). Branch from the step-3,200 checkpoint twice with the same data order: once restoring the saved AdamW state, once with a fresh AdamW and only the weights. One step later the validation loss is 1.560 for the correct branch and 1.622 for the weights-only branch, a jump of 0.061. The cause is Adam's bias correction: on the first step of a fresh optimizer the corrected averages are just $g$ and $g^2$, so the update is about $\eta \cdot g/|g|$, a full-size step of the peak LR for *every* weight, including weights whose gradient is tiny noise. With restored moments, those weights would have taken tiny steps.

blocks.title: Validation loss after the first steps of a branch from step 3,200

scenes.caption: Restoring weights, AdamW state and data order: the loss stays at the trunk's level (1.563) and starts to fall as the cooldown lowers the LR.
Weights only: one step costs 0.061 in loss, and 20 steps later the branch is still 0.011 behind.
At this tiny scale the damage washes out: after the full 800-step cooldown both branches end at about the same loss (1.490 vs 1.489). The spike is the symptom to look for.

blocks.md: Branch checklist: weights, optimizer state (including its step count), the global step that drives the LR schedule, and the data position. A loss spike on the first step of a branch means the optimizer state was not restored; a branch that starts with a warmup means the step counter was reset.

blocks.question: A cooldown branch shows a sharp loss jump on its very first step and then slowly recovers. The LR log shows the expected 1-sqrt decay from the peak. What was most likely left out of the restore?
options: The AdamW state (its moments and step count)
The data loader position
The model weights
The validation set
blocks.explain: With fresh moments, Adam's bias-corrected first update is about the LR times the sign of the gradient for every weight, a large uniform step. Missing weights would start from random init (a huge loss), and a wrong data position changes which batches are seen but does not cause a first-step jump.

blocks.question: Spot the bug: a branch for a 6,000-step model starts at step 4,800 and calls `run(m, opt, gen, 4800, 6000, lambda t: wsd(t, 4800, 6000))`. What happens?
options: Nothing: the decay length only matters for linear cooldowns
The cooldown is spread over 6,000 steps, so at step 6,000 the LR is still 1 - sqrt(0.2), about 0.55 of peak, and the model never anneals
The LR drops to zero immediately at step 4,800
The branch reruns warmup
blocks.explain: decay_len must be total - start = 1,200. With 6,000, the run stops when p = 1,200 / 6,000 = 0.2 of the way through the decay, at 1 - sqrt(0.2) = 0.553 of the peak: a half-annealed model, the same problem as stopping cosine early.

lessons.title: Cheap scaling studies, continual training and failure modes

blocks.md: The biggest payoff of WSD is for **scaling-law** experiments, the scaling studies met in the first lesson. Hägele et al. replicate a small study: model sizes from 33M to 360M parameters, each at 10, 20 and 30 tokens per parameter. With cosine, each model is trained three times from scratch. With a cooldown schedule, each model is trained once at constant LR, and three cooldowns (20% of each length, linear) are branched from it. The cooldown runs scaled as reliably as cosine.

blocks.title: Training cost for three data sizes of one model

scenes.caption: Cosine: three independent runs of 10, 20 and 30 tokens per parameter, each with T matched to its length. Total cost: 10 + 20 + 30 = 60 units.
WSD: one stable trunk to 24 (80% of the longest), plus 20% cooldowns branched at 8, 16 and 24. Total: 24 + 2 + 4 + 6 = 36 units, 0.6x the cosine cost.
Add a fourth size, 40 tokens per parameter. Cosine needs a new 40-unit run (total 100). WSD extends the trunk from 24 to 32 and adds an 8-unit cooldown: 16 more (total 52).

blocks.md: Scaled up, the savings grow with the number of lengths per model. Hägele et al. estimate that the Chinchilla model suite, under their assumed setup of four token ratios (10 to 25 tokens per parameter) per model, would cost $5.59\times10^{23}$ FLOPs with cosine, against $2.36\times10^{23}$ with one run per size plus 10% cooldowns, about 2.4x fewer. MiniCPM used this trick to fit the loss $L$ as a function of parameter count $N$ and training tokens $D$, from 6 model sizes (0.04B to 2B) with 6 decays each, and in their setup found a **compute-optimal** ratio (the tokens per parameter that gives the lowest loss for a fixed compute budget) of about 192 tokens per parameter, far above Chinchilla's roughly 20.

**Continual training.** Continuing from a pre-decay checkpoint at the same LR avoids the rewarming spikes that hurt cosine. Wen et al. go further with **WSD-S**, which their paper spells out as Warmup-Stable-Decay-Simplified. It resumes the trunk directly from the *decayed* checkpoint at the high LR, so the decay phases are not thrown away. On 0.1B to 1.2B parameter models with 50B, 100B and 200B token budgets, WSD-S beat WSD and cyclic cosine (a fresh cosine cycle, rewarmed to the peak, for each new budget), and matched cosine runs tuned separately for each budget.

Doesn't WSD-S rewarm a decayed model, which lesson 1 warned causes slow-recovering spikes after cosine? Wen et al. address this directly. They found that raising the LR after a *short* WSD decay does not cause the drop seen when cosine is rewarmed, and argue that the culprit with cosine is not the LR jump but a model that spent too long at a small LR, which they hypothesize is implicitly hurt for later training. In the river valley picture, the decay makes river progress as well as removing the hill; when the LR goes back up, the hill returns (in the toy, within about 100 steps), but the river progress stays. In their ablation on 0.6B models, swapping the second-half schedules showed that the run trained with WSD in the first half ended lower either way, and WSD-S beat cyclic cosine by 0.04 in loss at 100B tokens.

blocks.title: WSD vs WSD-S when you keep training

scenes.caption: Plain WSD: the 50B model branches off, and continued training rolls back to the last stable checkpoint. The work done during the decay is discarded.
WSD-S: continue straight from the decayed 50B model at the high LR. Only one checkpoint needs to be kept or released, and the decay's river progress is reused.

blocks.md: WSD is **not fully schedule-free**. Optimal peak LR still shifts with training length: Bergsma et al. (2025) quote Shen et al. puzzling that the best WSD LRs differ by token count, and Hägele et al. found the best cooldown peak LR was about half the best cosine peak. Tune the peak LR at roughly the length you care about; lesson 7 gives the evidence and a rule for adjusting it.

Other failure modes and limits reported in the sources:

- **If the length is known, linear decay to zero can win.** Bergsma et al. found linear decay-to-zero (D2Z) beat WSD by about 0.84% in loss for a 610M model at 80 tokens per parameter, though WSD beat linear decay to 10%.
- **Do not start a cooldown right after a loss spike.** Wen et al. saw validation loss worse by 0.02 when the decay began just after a spike; roll back a little or wait for the loss to recover.
- **Keep the pre-decay state.** Plain WSD continuation needs the stable checkpoint with its optimizer state (the optimizer's running averages from lesson 1), not just the released model; lesson 5 shows what goes wrong without it.
- **Averaging is a partial substitute.** Stochastic weight averaging (SWA), which averages the weights of recent checkpoints so that part of the bouncing cancels, on a constant LR closes much, but not all, of the gap to a real cooldown (Hägele et al.). Lesson 7 compares averaging and other cooldown-free options.

WSD separates *making progress* (long constant LR trunk) from *cashing it in* (short cooldown). That separation is what makes checkpoints reusable, runs extendable and scaling studies roughly linear in the number of model sizes instead of quadratic.

blocks.question: You must produce models at 4 data sizes for each of 5 model sizes. Which plan uses WSD correctly to minimize compute?
options: 20 runs from scratch, each with WSD and a 10% cooldown
1 run of the largest model, with cooldowns used to simulate the smaller models
5 cosine runs with T equal to the longest length, evaluated at 4 intermediate checkpoints
5 long constant LR runs (one per size), each with 4 cooldown branches from checkpoints
blocks.explain: Cooldowns replace the data axis, not the model axis: each model size still needs its own trunk. The cosine-checkpoint option is the classic mistake, since mid-run cosine checkpoints are not annealed and underestimate those lengths.

blocks.question: Your team knows the exact token budget for a one-off production run and will never extend it. Which statement best matches the evidence?
options: With a known budget, a well-tuned decay over the whole run (for example linear to zero) can match or slightly beat WSD; WSD's main advantage is flexibility
WSD is strictly required, because cosine cannot reach the same loss
WSD is always at least 10% better in loss
Any schedule is fine as long as there is warmup
blocks.explain: Hägele et al. found cooldowns roughly match tuned cosine, and Bergsma et al. found linear decay-to-zero about 0.84% better than WSD at 80 tokens per parameter. WSD shines when the end date is uncertain or many lengths are needed.

lessons.title: Other ways to drop the end date: averaging, schedule-free, theory

blocks.md: A cooldown removes the hill by lowering the LR. There is a second way to stop the bouncing from showing: **average** the weights. If one checkpoint sits a little up the left wall and a later one a little up the right wall, their average sits near the floor, while both have travelled the same distance down the river. Take the toy's constant-LR run at step 10,000 from lesson 3: loss 0.750 above the floor, of which the hill is 0.253. This lesson asks how much of that hill averaging can remove without ever lowering the LR, then looks at an optimizer built around averaging and at what convex optimization theory says about cooldowns.

Some names first. **Stochastic weight averaging (SWA)**, met briefly in lesson 6, averages the weights visited over a window of training. An **exponential moving average (EMA)** keeps a running average in which each step's weights get a fixed small share. **LAWA**, LAtest Weight Averaging (Kaddour, 2022; adapted to LLM pretraining by Sanyal et al., 2023), keeps a first-in first-out queue of the latest $k$ saved checkpoints, taken $\nu$ steps apart, and returns their plain average. None of them changes the training run itself: the average is a separate copy used for evaluation or release.

The average also lags: its river position is that of the middle checkpoint, $(k-1)\nu/2$ steps behind the latest one. So there is a trade. Close checkpoints cancel almost nothing, because a bounce lasts many steps; far-apart checkpoints cancel the hill but the average falls behind on the river. The figure computes both effects in the toy, using the same formula as lesson 3 for the river part.

blocks.caption: Hill of the average of k checkpoints spaced nu steps apart, in the toy's steep direction at constant LR. The bounce y is correlated from step to step by 1 - eta h = 0.98, so checkpoints nu steps apart have correlation rho. With rho near 1 nothing cancels; with rho near 0 the hill shrinks to H* / k.

blocks.title: Toy model, constant LR, step 10,000: averaging vs a cooldown

scenes.caption: Hill part only. Five consecutive checkpoints remove almost nothing (0.245 of 0.253): a bounce in the toy lasts about 50 steps. Spaced 200 apart, five checkpoints cut the hill to 0.052, ten to 0.026.

Total loss above the floor. The 5-checkpoint, 200-apart average (0.552) nearly matches the 10% cooldown (0.550) despite its 400-step river lag. Simplified: the toy has a single wall, which flatters averaging.

blocks.md: Real runs agree on the direction, not on the size. Sanyal et al. trained GPT-2 style models of 125M to 770M parameters on OpenWebText (an open recreation of the web text GPT-2 was trained on) and found that models trained with a higher LR gain more from LAWA, that sampling checkpoints far apart amplifies the gain, and that the averaged trajectory looks like a run with a lower LR. Hägele et al. ran SWA on a constant-LR 210M model: a strong improvement, but it did not reach the loss of an explicit cooldown (windows up to about 2,500 steps worked best; EMA did worse than SWA). ByteDance's study of model merging in pretraining (2025) forked a 1.3B-active, 13B-total mixture-of-experts model (one that sends each token through only a few of its many feed-forward blocks) at 1.4T tokens: merged constant-LR checkpoints beat the annealed branch early on and were comparable to it later. They also found merging helps less once models are annealed to a very low LR, because the checkpoints then sit in one narrow basin.

The same experiment on the tiny GPT from lesson 5. Train at a constant peak LR of 2e-3 for 6,000 steps, keep the weights every 50 steps, and average the last $k$ snapshots spaced $\nu$ steps apart. The last iterate has validation loss 1.539. Averaging 5 snapshots 100 apart gives 1.487, and 20 snapshots 100 apart 1.482. For comparison, lesson 5's 1,200-step cooldown from step 4,800 reached 1.492, and the 6,000-step cosine run 1.513.

blocks.title: Tiny GPT at step 6,000: averaging vs cooldown (loss above 1.40)

scenes.caption: Validation loss, one seed. Here averaging matches the cooldown (differences of about 0.01 are within run-to-run noise) at zero extra training steps. Hägele et al.'s 210M LLM runs still showed a gap, so do not expect this everywhere.

blocks.md: **Schedule-Free AdamW** (Defazio et al., 2024) builds the averaging into the optimizer. It keeps three sequences. $z$ is the base sequence that takes the raw optimizer steps at a constant LR $\gamma$. $x$ is the running average of all the $z$ points, the weights you evaluate. $y$, where the gradient is computed, is an interpolation of the two, controlled by $\beta$ (around 0.9, playing the role of momentum; in the AdamW version it is the first entry of `betas`, and the second is Adam's usual $\beta_2$). Because $x$ is a uniform average with weight $c_{t+1} = 1/(t+1)$, nothing in the update depends on the stopping step $T$.

blocks.caption: Schedule-Free SGD. zeta t is the random minibatch. beta = 0 gives Polyak-Ruppert averaging (gradients at z, average returned) and beta = 1 primal averaging (gradients at the average). The AdamW version applies an Adam step to z and weights c by the squared warmup LR.

blocks.md:
Practical points from the paper and its code:

- **No extra memory over AdamW.** Two of the three sequences are stored and the third is computed from them; the $z$ buffer takes the place of Adam's momentum buffer.
- **Mode switching.** Training uses $y$ and evaluation uses $x$, so you call `optimizer.train()` and `optimizer.eval()` next to `model.train()` and `model.eval()`, and save checkpoints in eval mode. BatchNorm statistics must be recomputed at $x$.
- **Still tuned.** Warmup is still needed, and LR and weight decay must be swept again; the authors report the best values differ from scheduled AdamW. $\beta$ matters more than ordinary momentum.
- **Results.** It won the self-tuning track of the AlgoPerf 2024 challenge run by MLCommons, the industry and academic group behind the MLPerf benchmarks,, where one hyperparameter setting must work on 8 workloads. In Hägele et al.'s 210M LLM test it was sensitive to its $(\beta_1, \beta_2)$: $(0.9, 0.95)$ was clearly worse, $(0.95, 0.99)$ remarkably good, and the cooldown schedule matched or beat both.

blocks.code:
import schedulefree
opt = schedulefree.AdamWScheduleFree(model.parameters(), lr=lr, betas=(0.95, 0.99),
                                     weight_decay=0.1, warmup_steps=100)
model.train(); opt.train()               # parameters now hold y
for step in range(N):
    loss = model(*next_batch()); opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    if step + 1 in eval_steps:
        opt.eval()                        # swap in x, the average
        val = evaluate(model)            # also save checkpoints here
        opt.train()
blocks.caption: The Schedule-Free AdamW loop used for the run below (schedulefree package from the paper's repository). No scheduler object; the only schedule is the built-in warmup.

blocks.title: Schedule-Free AdamW at three lengths (val loss above 1.40)

scenes.caption: Step 2,000: one Schedule-Free run per LR, evaluated at its average x; WSD and cosine at peak 2e-3. With LR 8e-3, 4x the scheduled peak, it reaches 1.563, below WSD (1.575) and cosine (1.625). At 2e-3 it lags far behind (1.775).

Step 4,000: one Schedule-Free run per LR, evaluated at its average x; WSD and cosine at peak 2e-3. 8e-3: 1.504 vs WSD 1.501 and cosine 1.525. Schedule-Free needed its own LR sweep, as its authors warn.

Step 6,000: one Schedule-Free run per LR, evaluated at its average x; WSD and cosine at peak 2e-3. 8e-3: 1.495 vs WSD 1.492 and cosine 1.513, from one run with no cooldown. The sweep stopped at 8e-3, so a higher LR might do better.

blocks.md: Why do cooldowns work at all? Schaipp et al. (2025) took a bound from **non-smooth convex optimization**: the theory of SGD on convex losses (bowl-shaped, with no separate local minima) that need not be smooth, with gradient norm at most $G$ and starting distance $D$ from the optimum. The bound (from Defazio et al., 2023) limits the loss of the *last* iterate for any LR schedule. Plotted over training, it has the same shape as real LLM loss curves, including the sudden drop when a WSD cooldown starts, even though LLM losses are not convex. For a constant LR the bound carries a factor $1 + H_{T-1}$, where $H_t = 1 + \frac12 + \dots + \frac1t$ is the harmonic number (no relation to the hill $H$ earlier in this lesson), which grows like $\ln t$. With a linear cooldown over a fixed fraction of training, the log term cancels: the benefit of the cooldown shows up in theory as a missing $\ln T$.

blocks.caption: Schaipp et al.'s bound for a constant schedule with the base LR tuned for the horizon T. At T = 100,000, 1 + H is about 13.1, so the bound is about 3.62 DG over root T.

blocks.title: Convex bound at T = 100,000 (D = G = 1), tuned base LR

scenes.caption: Bound times root T, computed from Schaipp et al.'s Corollary 3.3. Constant 3.62; a 20% cooldown brings it to 2.16, close to cosine (2.06) and linear decay to zero (2.00), the best of the five.
The tuned base LR times root T. Cosine's best LR (0.97) is about 1.9x WSD's (0.51), matching lesson 6's observation that the best cooldown peak is about half the best cosine peak.

blocks.md: Two consequences. First, in this theory the tuned base LR scales like $1/\sqrt T$: a longer run wants a smaller peak, which is why lesson 6 warns that WSD is not fully schedule-free. Bjorck et al. (2025) measured the same effect in GPT-3 style models of 50M to 2.7B parameters trained with cosine: the optimal LR falls as a power law in the token horizon $D$, $\mathrm{LR}^*(D) = B\,D^{-\beta}$, and recommend $\beta \approx 0.32$ for models of about 760M parameters and up. Doubling the tokens then multiplies the best LR by $2^{-0.32} \approx 0.80$. Their fit suggests LLaMA-1 7B, trained at $3\times10^{-4}$, would have done better at about $1.15\times10^{-4}$ for 1T tokens.

Second, the theory says how to extend a WSD run. Suppose the peak was tuned for $T_1$ steps and you now want $T_2 = 2T_1$. Continuing at the same peak is too high for the longer horizon. For a 20% cooldown, Schaipp et al.'s bound suggests dropping the LR to 0.525 of the peak from the point where the short run's cooldown would have started (0.375 for $T_2 = 4T_1$), keeping all the constant-LR steps already done. On 124M and 210M Llama-style models extended from 50k to 100k and 200k steps, this slightly but noticeably beat continuing at the original LR.

blocks.prompt: Your WSD peak LR of 6e-4 was tuned on a 50B-token proxy run. The production run will see 200B tokens. Using Bjorck et al.'s exponent of 0.32, roughly what peak should you start the sweep around?
blocks.reveal: $6\times10^{-4} \times 4^{-0.32} \approx 6\times10^{-4}\times 0.64 \approx 3.9\times10^{-4}$. Treat it as the centre of a small sweep, not a final answer: the exponent was fitted on cosine runs of GPT-3 style models, and Bjorck et al. found a larger exponent for their smallest models.

scenes.caption: A one-off run with a known budget: a decay spread over the whole run, linear to zero, was best in Bergsma et al. and is optimal for the convex bound.
Unknown end date, planned extensions or a scaling study: WSD, with the peak LR set for the horizon you care about most.
No cooldown at all, for example a model that must be usable at every checkpoint: averaging or Schedule-Free AdamW. Expect them to come close to a cooldown, and sometimes fall short.

blocks.md: A cooldown, a checkpoint average and Schedule-Free's running average all do the same job: they stop the high-LR bouncing from showing in the weights you evaluate. They differ in what they cost (extra steps, extra copies, retuning) and in whether the training run must know its end date.

blocks.question: You average the last 5 checkpoints of a constant-LR run, saved every 10 steps, and see almost no improvement. In the river valley picture, what is the most likely reason?
options: Averaging can only work after a cooldown
The checkpoints are too close together: the bouncing is correlated over many steps, so they all sit on the same side of the wall
Five checkpoints are too many; averaging two would cancel more
Averaging moves the model backwards along the river by 50 steps, erasing the gain
blocks.explain: With correlation rho near 1 between checkpoints, the average keeps almost all the hill (in the toy, 5 checkpoints 10 steps apart keep 74% of it, and 5 consecutive ones 97%). Spacing them out, as LAWA does, makes their bounces independent. The river lag of 20 steps here is negligible.

blocks.question: A teammate switches to Schedule-Free AdamW, keeps the LR and weight decay tuned for cosine AdamW, and evaluates the parameters stored in the model during training. Which two problems should you point out?
options: None: Schedule-Free needs no tuning and the stored parameters are the average
Schedule-Free needs a cosine schedule on top, and it doubles memory
It cannot use warmup, and checkpoints must be saved in train mode
The LR and weight decay need a new sweep, and without optimizer.eval() the model holds y, the gradient point, rather than the average x
blocks.explain: The authors report the best LR and weight decay differ from scheduled runs, and their code stores y in the parameter buffer during training; optimizer.eval() swaps in x for evaluation and checkpointing. Warmup is still used, and memory matches AdamW.
